nameStory: Baird's Sandpiper honors Spencer Fullerton Baird, a 19th-century naturalist who served as assistant secretary of the Smithsonian Institution. Baird was a passionate bird collector and researcher who helped establish many of America's natural history collections, making this small shorebird a fitting tribute to his dedication to understanding our feathered friends.
description: Baird's Sandpiper is a small, brownish shorebird about the size of a sparrow that visits New England's beaches and mudflats during migration. These compact little birds have relatively long wings that extend past their tail when folded, giving them a streamlined appearance. They're part of the challenging group of small sandpipers that birders affectionately call 'peeps' because of their high-pitched calls. With their buff-brown coloring and quick, darting movements, they blend seamlessly into sandy shorelines as they probe for tiny invertebrates.

idTips.label: Wing Length
idTips.description: Wings extend noticeably past the tail tip when folded, creating a distinctive long-winged silhouette that's longer than most other small sandpipers

idTips.label: Back Pattern
idTips.description: Feathers on the back have dark centers with buff or pale edges, creating a scaly appearance that looks like tiny overlapping scales

idTips.label: Bill Shape
idTips.description: Straight, dark bill that's neither as thin as a Least Sandpiper's nor as thick as a Semipalmated Sandpiper's - feels sturdy if you were to touch it

idTips.label: Leg Color
idTips.description: Dark blackish legs that stand out against light sand, unlike the yellowish legs of Least Sandpipers

idTips.label: Overall Coloring
idTips.description: Rich buff-brown tones, especially on the breast and face, giving it a warmer appearance than the grayer Semipalmated Sandpiper

habitat: Look for Baird's Sandpipers on sandy beaches, mudflats, and the edges of coastal ponds and marshes throughout New England's coastline. They prefer areas where waves have left behind wet sand or mud that's perfect for probing, often feeding just above the high-tide line where small crustaceans and marine worms are abundant. Unlike some sandpipers, they occasionally venture to inland locations like the muddy edges of reservoirs and flooded fields.

seasonality.spring: Present during May migration, though less common than in fall. Adults may show fresher breeding plumage with more distinct markings and brighter buff tones.
seasonality.summer: Rarely seen, as they breed far north in the Arctic tundra. Any summer sightings would likely be non-breeding individuals.
seasonality.fall: Most commonly observed from late July through September during southward migration. Juveniles show crisp, fresh plumage while adults may appear more worn.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England, having continued south to wintering grounds in South America.

funFact: Baird's Sandpipers are incredible long-distance migrants that can fly nonstop for over 2,000 miles, traveling from their Arctic breeding grounds all the way to South America - some individuals making a journey equivalent to flying from New York to Denver without landing once!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Semipalmated and Least Sandpipers, the other common 'peeps.' Remember: Baird's has dark legs (not yellow like Least) and longer wings that stick out past the tail (unlike the shorter-winged Semipalmated). Think 'Baird's has long wings for long flights.'
contextualKnowledge: Baird's Sandpiper represents one of many bird species named after Spencer Baird, who described numerous North American birds in the 1800s. The scientific naming reflects the old tradition of honoring prominent naturalists, making this species part of living history that connects us to early American ornithology.
compareHints: Among the small Calidris sandpipers, Baird's stands out with its notably long wing projection past the tail - much longer than Semipalmated or Least Sandpipers. It's buffer and warmer-toned than the grayer Semipalmated Sandpiper, and larger overall than the tiny Least Sandpiper. The White-rumped Sandpiper also has long wings, but shows a distinctive white rump patch in flight that Baird's lacks.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the Calidris sandpipers, sanderlings are notably stockier with a thicker bill than the needle-billed Least Sandpiper or Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Within the Calidris genus, Semipalmated Sandpipers are most similar to Western Sandpipers but have blunter, shorter bills and less rusty coloring in breeding plumage.
Among its Calidris cousins, the Least Sandpiper's yellow-green legs immediately set it apart from the black-legged Semipalmated and Sanderling.

Among the Calidris sandpipers, dunlin are larger than the "peeps" (semipalmated, least, and white-rumped sandpipers) but smaller than red knot, with that diagnostic curved bill that none of the others possess.
Among the many Calidris sandpipers, Purple Sandpiper is unique for its consistently dark plumage and exclusive rocky habitat preference.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, White-rumped is most similar to Baird's Sandpiper, but Baird's lacks the white rump and has a more buff-colored breast.

Among the Calidris sandpipers in New England, pectoral sandpipers are distinguished by their larger size and that signature sharp breast line - dunlin have curved bills and different streaking, while the various 'peeps' (least, semipalmated) are much smaller.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, Red Knot is the second-largest and most robust, much chunkier than Sanderling or Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Among New England's Calidris sandpipers, the Stilt Sandpiper is the tallest and longest-legged, easily distinguished from the tiny 'peeps' like Least and Semipalmated Sandpipers.
Among New England's Calidris sandpipers, Buff-breasted is unique for its solid peachy-tan underparts and preference for grassy areas over mudflats.

Among New England's small sandpipers, Western Sandpipers are most easily confused with Semipalmated Sandpipers, but Westerns have longer, more drooped bill tips and often show more rusty coloring in breeding plumage.
Among Calidris sandpipers, Ruffs are unique in their extreme sexual size difference - much more pronounced than in Dunlin or Pectoral Sandpipers.
Among its Calidris sandpiper relatives, the Curlew Sandpiper's curved bill immediately sets it apart from straight-billed species like Sanderling and Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Among its Calidris relatives in New England, Little Stint is smaller than Least Sandpiper (already our tiniest regular sandpiper) and much smaller than Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Compared to other small Calidris sandpipers in New England, Red-necked Stint is smaller than Semipalmated Sandpiper and has darker legs than Least Sandpiper.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, Sharp-tailed is most similar to Pectoral Sandpiper in size and habitat preferences, but lacks the Pectoral's sharply cut breast band.
Among Calidris sandpipers, the Surfbird is uniquely stocky and rock-adapted, unlike its beach and mudflat-loving relatives.
